title: Levi bar Buta
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He is mentioned in [Megillah 31b](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.31b.9): he was reading the curses (Arurei) before Rav Huna and was stammering; he said to him, “As you wish” [אכנפשך], etc.

And in the [Jerusalem Talmud there, chapter 3, halakhah 7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Megillah.3.7.2), it reads: ‘Levi bar Pasti asked Rav Chuna: These arurya (curses), how are they to be read—as one?’ etc.; Hyman takes this to be the same statement as in the Babylonian Talmud. In [Soferim, chapter 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Tractate_Soferim.12.3), the statement is brought in the name of bar Pati, who asked R' Chanina. In [Kohelet Rabbah, chapter 8-3](https://www.sefaria.org/Kohelet_Rabbah.8.3.1), the statement is brought: ‘R' Levi bar Panti read the arurya before R' Chuna and stammered over them.’ It appears to Hyman that this is the correct reading; as for what crept into the Babylonian Talmud under the name of Rav Huna, Hyman says it should read R' Huna. In the Jerusalem Talmud he is called R' Chuna.

Hyman says that in Seder HaDorot (printed: סה״ד) they divided him into two, under the entries [Levi bar Buta](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=2338&lang=en) and [Levi ben Panti](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=2345&lang=en), and he did not notice that it is all one man.[^3]

notes.text: אכנפשך remains an unexplained quoted instruction. Buta/Buti, Pasti, Pati and Panti are distinct reported forms. Hyman argues for a Palestinian Rabbi Huna rather than the Babylonian Rav Huna; his own quotation uses both titles, and the tension remains visible.

The whole saved Davidson Megillah 31b scalar reads Levi bar Buti before full Rav Huna; the whole selected Vilna Rashi gloss explains אכנפשך as permission to stop if the reader wishes, because he is distressed by the reading. As you wish translates the instruction locally; no unselected Rashi comment on hurried reading or additional legal continuation is imported. Buta/Buti, Pasti/Pati/Panti and Chuna/Huna remain different written forms, and bar versus ben is retained. Hyman’s quoted full Rav Chuna and his final R-prime Chuna remain in tension. The five abbreviated personal-title occurrences in p 003 are rendered R-prime, correcting the unsupported full Rabbi forms in the current body and qualifying its older note additively; the three explicit full Rav occurrences remain full. It appears preserves ונראה, while should read preserves the directed צ״ל correction as Hyman’s claim, not a title repair established by the Davidson passage. The question how-to-read-as-one, all etc. cutoffs, Yerushalmi 3 halakhah 7, Soferim 12 and literal Kohelet Rabbah 8-3 remain. No first name or missing-text marker is supplied before bar Pati. The contextual Seder HaDorot expansion, they divided/he did not notice alternation and all-one-man assertion remain Hyman’s argument, not an authority merger. The older unexplained-instruction note is retained as history and qualified by these named digital readings; its other variant and title cautions remain. The selected digital texts are not printed-image or correction-history proof. The source hold remains unchanged.

The linked Bavli has bar Buti and Rav Huna. [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Megillah.31b.9.3) explains the reply as permission to stop if distressed. The Yerushalmi and Soferim name bar Pati, with Rav Chuna and R’ Chanina respectively. Kohelet Rabbah has ben Panti and Rabbi Huna. Heilprin gives separate entries. Hyman argues that the narratives concern one person.
